about: MDosce picks: featured playlists (founder 2026-10-28: 'set up some Qs packs by searching online and putting them as playlist options'). Original questions written for MDosce from open Australian guidelines, read 2026-10-28; no question is copied from any bank. Each pack names its sources; check the current guideline before acting on a dose.

packs.title: Paeds acute: the RCH essentials
packs.blurb: Croup, bronchiolitis and anaphylaxis, the way the RCH guidelines run them. For a paeds placement or ED shift.
packs.source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines: Croup, Bronchiolitis, Anaphylaxis

questions.stem: A 3-year-old has a barking cough and stridor at rest, with mild recession, but is alert and pink. What is the first treatment?
questions.explanation: Moderate croup: an oral steroid (dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg, or prednisolone 1 mg/kg). Nebulised adrenaline is added if symptoms persist or worsen.
why: Moderate croup is treated with an oral steroid.
Croup is upper airway; bronchodilators do not help.
Croup is viral: antibiotics have no role.
Humidified air has not been shown to change severity.
Anti-tussives do not help and can depress breathing.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old with croup is drowsy and pale, with biphasic stridor and marked sternal recession. What do you give now?
questions.explanation: Severe or life-threatening croup: nebulised adrenaline (5 mL of 1:1000), oxygen, dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg (max 12 mg), and a senior clinician for the airway.
why: Nebulised adrenaline buys time in severe croup.
A steroid alone is too slow for a threatened airway.
Not the treatment for severe obstruction.
Examining the throat can precipitate complete obstruction.

questions.stem: A child with croup improves after nebulised adrenaline. How long must they be observed before going home?
questions.explanation: Observe for at least 3 hours after nebulised adrenaline: symptoms can return as it wears off. Discharge once stridor free at rest.
why: Too short: the rebound comes later.
Longer stays are for risk factors, not everyone.
Adrenaline wears off; the stridor can return.

questions.stem: Which sign in croup is the most worrying for imminent airway obstruction?
options: Soft stridor with a worsening child
questions.explanation: Loudness of stridor is a poor guide. Soft stridor in a child who is getting worse can mean little air is moving. Hypoxia is a late sign.
why: Quiet stridor in a tiring child means little air moving.
Stridor only when upset is mild.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old with bronchiolitis has brief dips to 88% that recover; otherwise SpO2 is 92 to 94%. What is right about oxygen?
options: No oxygen: start only if SpO2 stays below 90%
Give oxygen whenever SpO2 is below 94%
questions.explanation: Target SpO2 is 90% or more. Brief dips are expected in bronchiolitis and are not a reason to start oxygen. Nasal prongs only for persistent SpO2 below 90%.
why: Brief dips are expected; the trigger is persistent < 90%.
High flow is for failure of low-flow oxygen.

questions.stem: In typical bronchiolitis, which of these does the RCH guideline recommend?
options: Supportive care: hydration and oxygen as needed
questions.explanation: Bronchiolitis is a clinical diagnosis and treatment is supportive: keep the infant hydrated and oxygenated, with minimal handling. Investigations only for deterioration or diagnostic doubt.
why: Not indicated; it leads to needless antibiotics.
Viral; fever alone is not a reason.

questions.stem: Which infant with bronchiolitis is at higher risk of deteriorating?
questions.explanation: Risk factors include prematurity (under 37 weeks), age under 10 weeks, congenital heart or chronic lung disease, neurological conditions, trisomy 21, Indigenous ethnicity and smoke exposure.
why: Two risk factors: preterm and under 10 weeks.
Eczema is not a listed risk factor.
Peak is usually day 2 to 3, but this alone is not a risk factor.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old (16 kg) with peanut allergy has hives, wheeze and a hoarse voice. What do you give first?
options: IM adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg into the lateral thigh
questions.explanation: Anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline, 0.01 mg/kg (0.01 mL/kg of 1:1000), lateral thigh, repeated every 5 minutes if needed. In a child with asthma, adrenaline comes first, then asthma medicines.
why: IM is absorbed more reliably than subcutaneous.

questions.stem: A child with anaphylaxis wants to get up after IM adrenaline. What is the right advice?
options: Stay lying flat or sitting with legs out
Walk to the bathroom with help
Any position is fine once the rash fades
questions.explanation: Position matters: lay the child flat, or sitting with legs extended. Do not let them stand or walk for at least an hour after symptoms settle.
why: Not for at least an hour after symptoms settle.
Upright with legs down risks collapse.
The danger lasts longer than the rash.

questions.stem: Which adrenaline autoinjector suits a 3-year-old weighing 15 kg?
questions.explanation: The 150 microgram device (EpiPen Jr) is for 7.5 to 20 kg; 300 microgram for over 20 kg; 500 microgram for over 50 kg.
why: One device; repeat after 5 minutes if needed.

packs.title: Fever, fluids and jaundice in the young
packs.blurb: The febrile infant, dehydration sums and the jaundice that is not physiological.
packs.source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines: Febrile child, Dehydration, Jaundice in early infancy

questions.stem: A 15-day-old has a temperature of 38.2 °C but looks well and is feeding. What does she need?
options: Full septic work-up and empirical IV antibiotics
Discharge if the CRP is normal
questions.explanation: Febrile infants 21 days or younger need a full septic work-up (FBE, CRP, blood, urine and CSF cultures, with or without CXR) and empirical IV antibiotics, whatever they look like.
why: Required at this age regardless of appearance.
A normal CRP does not exclude infection here.
A viral result does not exclude bacterial infection.

questions.stem: What is the most common serious bacterial infection in febrile children?
questions.explanation: UTI is the most common serious bacterial infection in febrile children, which is why a clean urine sample is part of assessing them.

questions.stem: Which best predicts serious illness in a febrile 2-year-old?
options: Whether the fever falls with paracetamol
questions.explanation: Severity cannot be predicted by the degree of fever or its response to antipyretics. Age, appearance and behaviour are the better guides.
why: Appearance and behaviour are the best indicators.
Do not blame fever on vaccination in an unwell child.
Do not blame fever on teething in an unwell child.

questions.stem: A child weighed 10 kg two weeks ago and now weighs 9.5 kg after gastroenteritis. What is the deficit?
questions.explanation: The weight lost is the water lost: 0.5 kg is 500 mL, which is 5% of 10 kg. A recent weight is the most accurate measure of dehydration.
why: Out by a factor of ten.
The volume is wrong: 0.5 kg is 500 mL.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old with gastroenteritis is moderately dehydrated but not shocked. How should you rehydrate?
options: Enterally: oral, or by nasogastric tube
questions.explanation: Rehydrate enterally (by mouth or nasogastric tube) unless dehydration is severe or the child is in shock. Shock needs prompt IV fluid boluses.
why: Not the first choice without shock.
Small frequent amounts work despite vomiting.
Sugary drinks can worsen diarrhoea and sodium balance.

questions.stem: Which jaundiced newborn needs urgent assessment?
options: Jaundice first seen at 18 hours old
Jaundice on day 3 in a well, feeding baby
Jaundice in a breastfed baby on day 5 with yellow stools
questions.explanation: Jaundice in the first 24 hours is pathological until proven otherwise (often haemolysis). Most jaundice after that in a well baby is physiological.
why: Onset under 24 hours is a red flag.

questions.stem: A 4-week-old is still jaundiced and has pale, chalky stools. What must be excluded urgently?
questions.explanation: Pale (acholic) stools at any age need urgent evaluation for cholestatic liver disease, including biliary atresia, with a conjugated bilirubin.
why: Pale stools signal cholestasis; outcome depends on early surgery.
Does not last to 4 weeks with pale stools.

questions.stem: How should you judge the bilirubin level of a jaundiced 2-day-old?
options: A transcutaneous or serum bilirubin, on a gestation-specific chart
By how far down the body the yellow spreads
By the colour of the sclerae
By the colour of the urine
questions.explanation: Visual assessment is unreliable (and harder on darker skin). Measure transcutaneous or serum bilirubin, and plot it on a gestation- and age-specific nomogram.
why: Measured and plotted against gestation and age.
A risk factor, not a measure.
Not a measure of the level.

packs.title: O&G: hypertension in pregnancy
packs.blurb: Severe BP, magnesium, and when to deliver, from the Victorian maternity guidance and SOMANZ.
packs.source: Safer Care Victoria Maternity eHandbook: Hypertension in pregnancy (citing the SOMANZ 2023 guideline)

questions.stem: At 34 weeks, a woman's BP is 164/112 on repeat. What is the main reason to treat it now?
questions.explanation: Severe hypertension (sustained 160/110 or more) is an emergency: treat urgently because of the risk of intracerebral haemorrhage.
why: The reason severe BP is treated urgently.

questions.stem: What defines severe hypertension in pregnancy?
options: Sustained BP of 160/110 mmHg or more
questions.explanation: Severe: sustained systolic 160 or more, or diastolic 110 or more. Hypertension in pregnancy is 140/90 or more.
why: A rise alone is not the definition.

questions.stem: Which antihypertensive should NOT be used in pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Labetalol, nifedipine and methyldopa are the oral agents for stable hypertension; hydralazine is used IV for severe BP. ACE inhibitors such as ramipril harm fetal kidneys.
why: ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy.

questions.stem: A woman at 36 weeks with pre-eclampsia has a seizure on the ward. What is the first-line treatment?
questions.explanation: A seizure in pregnancy is presumed eclampsia: magnesium sulfate is first line, with airway care. Then stabilise and plan birth.

questions.stem: When is birth indicated for stable pre-eclampsia with a well fetus?
questions.explanation: In pre-eclampsia, birth is indicated at 37 weeks. Before that, manage expectantly while mother and baby are stable, delivering sooner if either is compromised.

questions.stem: At 33 weeks with pre-eclampsia, which finding is an indication for birth?
questions.explanation: Indications include thrombocytopenia, eclampsia, severe intractable headache or visual scotomata, repeated severe BP despite several drugs, pulmonary oedema, rising creatinine or liver enzymes, abruption, or fetal compromise.
why: Thrombocytopenia is an indication for birth.
A severe, intractable headache would be.

questions.stem: Hypertension found at 12 weeks is most likely to be:
questions.explanation: Hypertension before 20 weeks is chronic (pre-existing). Gestational hypertension and pre-eclampsia arise after 20 weeks.
why: Possible, but not to be assumed.
A late, severe form of pre-eclampsia.

questions.stem: A woman with pre-eclampsia is likely to deliver at 28 weeks. Why give magnesium sulfate?
questions.explanation: Magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection is strongly recommended before 30 weeks; at 30 to 34 weeks it is decided case by case. Steroids, not magnesium, mature the lungs.
why: Before 30 weeks it protects the fetal brain.
Not used as a tocolytic here.
